The same three filters, fed by the two decodes.

Top: VAE Decode, whose highlights are already a flat 1.0 before the first filter runs. Its preview panel reads 'over white 0.00%'.

Bottom: HDR VAE Decode. Saturation, a bilateral median and a half-size resample all pass the range on, so the preview panel still reads a range above 1.0 and a share of the frame over white.

Read the 'range' and 'over white' rows on the two Image Preview panels. Same filters, same settings, different input.
a dark stone chapel interior at noon, one tall window blown out with sunlight, dust in the beam, deep shadow in the corners

STEP 1  The source

An 8-bit frame with two faults on purpose. The sky holds 95 distinct values over 768 rows, so it steps every 8 rows. The sun clips flat over 17% of the frame. The scene it came from peaked at 13.7; the file can only hold 1.0.

STEP 2  Dequantise

Rebuilds the levels between the codes. It never moves a sample by more than half a code, so it adds nothing: it recovers the gradient the quantiser flattened.

STEP 3  Reconstruct, then export

HDR Reconstruct infers what the clipped sun held. The first preview still clips, because a preview cannot show above 1.0. Image Preview reads the same data as light and drops it three stops, where the sun and its glow separate again.

EXR Save writes the real values. DNG Save writes them as 16-bit linear readings a raw developer opens.

STEP 4  Read the plate back

Queue the graph once so step 3 writes a file, then pick it in EXR Load. The values come back exactly as they were written, above one and all, which is what the same three stops showing the same sun proves.

alpha is white here, because the file holds no fourth channel.
